item.title: Trump prosecutions under Biden set precedent for DOJ’s Alaska ‘Decoy Dan’ probe, ex-FEC chair says
item.description: Hans von Spakovsky says Jack Smith's Trump indictment set the precedent for the DOJ's criminal probe into Alaska's "Decoy Dan" Senate race scheme.
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department is investigating allegations that Democratic operatives recruited Alaska Senate candidate Daniel J. Sullivan, dubbed "Decoy Dan," to siphon votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan—prompting liberal-leaning election-law experts to accuse the Trump administration of federal overreach.

But former Federal Election Commission member Hans von Spakovsky argued that the Biden-era Justice Department’s prosecution of Donald Trump over alleged efforts to overturn the 2020 election laid the groundwork for the Alaska probe.

"The Justice Department has talked about a potential conspiracy to defraud the voters of Alaska and people are saying, 'Oh, he's got no case. That's a weak case,'" Spakovsky, senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, told Fox News Digital. "Well, I suggest you do a Google search and pull up the indictment that Jack Smith got against Donald Trump in the District of Columbia. He set a precedent for this."

Joined by FBI officials and Alaska State Troopers, Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman announced at a Friday press conference that the Justice Department has been investigating whether Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired school teacher who will appear on the ballot without a party affiliation, was colluding with Democratic operatives tied to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola's campaign.

The Justice Department previously sued Alaska election officials, seeking to block certification if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses re-election by fewer votes than those cast for Daniel J. Sullivan. The lawsuit was amended Friday to include reporting by The New York Times that the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and senior aides of Peltola's campaign allegedly worked to recruit candidates who could pull votes away from Sen. Sulllivan. Heyman mentioned the Times reporting repeatedly in the press conference.

MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT

"We are taking that extremely seriously," Hetman said.

Sources at the Justice Department told Fox News Thursday that the Trump administration had issued more than 30 subpoeanas in a span of 24 hours as part of its criminal investigation into the alleged collusion, but Heyman did not say at the press conference what criminal charges are being pursued.

"I'm not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not," Heyman said. "That's why we are conducting that thorough investigation."

Von Spakovsky, a former Federal Election Commission commissioner, said potential indictments of Democratic operatives in the Alaska Senate race could rely on federal statutes similar to those Smith, the former special counsel, used in his 2023 indictment of Trump over alleged efforts to overturn the election.

Spakovsky pointed to charges of conspiracy to defraud the United States and conspiracy against rights. In Trump’s case, prosecutors alleged that he used fraud and deceit to obstruct the federal government’s process for certifying the 2020 election and conspired to deprive voters of having their lawful votes counted and honored.

Spakovsky said prosecutors could potentially apply similar theories in Alaska if they determine that Democratic operatives knowingly recruited Daniel J. Sullivan to confuse voters and divert votes from Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

ALASKA'S GOVERNOR ORDERS INVESTIGATION AFTER NYT REPORT ON ALLEGED DEM-LINKED SENATE ELECTION SCHEME

Smith's "indictment is basically along exactly those same lines, claiming that that Donald Trump was trying to defraud U.S. voters from fair and honest elections. So Jack Smith and Democrats, they set the precedent for the kind of investigation Justice Department is doing now."

Aubrey Wieber, executive director of 907 Initiative, a progressive advocacy group running critical ads against Sen. Sullivan, told Alaska Public Media that the press conference announcing the investigation "on the eve of the election" may be stemming from ulterior motives.

"One could say it appears that they are trying to interfere in an election and put their thumb on the scale," Wieber said.

The Justice Department's lawsuit was filed on Oct. 22, prompting a parade of condemnations from those who argued the federal government had "no authority" to intervene, with many pointing to the Alaska Supreme Court rejecting the state's push to disqualify Daniel J. Sullivan from appearing on the ballot.

GOVERNOR PROBING 'DECOY DAN' SULLIVAN ELECTION SCANDAL WARNS SYSTEM FLAW HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT

"DOJ's theory: two candidates named Sullivan might confuse voters. The Alaska Supreme Court settled that in June and the ballot labels the incumbent. DOJ has no role in state election law," Omar Noureldin, senior vice president of policy and litigation at Common Cause of Common Cause, a self-described no-partisan watchdog organization.

Spakovsky called recruiting a candidate with the same name as a political opponent a "dirty trick," but said the recruitment itself was not necessarily a criminal violation. He said the legal analysis could change if operatives paid the candidate or provided services to help organize his campaign.

"The place you run into potential issues is not only if you just recruit a candidate, but you’re being paid to recruit that candidate, and you then provide services to help him run his campaign and organize it," Spakovsky said.

Providing campaign assistance outside of being a volunteer is an in-kind contribution subject to federal reporting and contribution rules. Spakovsky said any failure to properly report such contributions could create a separate campaign-finance violation.

item.title: Maine school official raises Muslim religious objections to classroom dogs as district weighs policy changes
item.description: Dr. Abdullahi Ahmed cited Islamic beliefs about dog saliva as impure during a Portland Public Schools policy committee meeting on classroom pets.
item.content:encoded:
A Maine public school administrator raised concerns about allowing dogs in classrooms because of Islamic religious beliefs about the animals, as the district considers changes to its classroom pet policy following a teacher's request to foster puppies.

Dr. Abdullahi Ahmed, Portland Public Schools' assistant superintendent for student, family and community partnerships, discussed the concerns during an Oct. 14 policy committee meeting, explaining that some Islamic traditions consider dog saliva impure. Ahmed said he had consulted local Muslim religious leaders who opposed keeping dogs as classroom pets, according to a report by The National News Desk.

The debate began after a teacher at Ocean Avenue Elementary School sought permission to foster puppies in her classroom, giving students an opportunity to interact with the animals during reading and playtime. Ahmed suggested that accommodations could include keeping dogs in a separate room to respect students and families with religious objections.

ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW

Ahmed said that Muslim community members are not opposed to animals, saying, "in Islamic tradition, there is always the love for animals and living things and compassion for animals."

He went on to say that some Islamic traditions consider dogs unclean.

"So, with that being said, there are some ritual kind of a purity or in that Islamic traditions ... So, for example, the dog saliva is considered impure," Ahmed said. "And also some people had some experiences with dogs, which were negative actually in the past."

NEW YORK TIMES ACCUSED OF FRAMING MUSLIMS AS TRUE VICTIMS OF 9/11 IN ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE

Ahmed, who was born and raised in Somalia, speaks Somali, Arabic, English and Urdu, according to his district biography. He also said the imams he spoke with did not want dogs kept as pets in classrooms.

Committee members discussed whether any revised policy should apply only to dogs or extend to other classroom animals, along with potential opt-in and opt-out accommodations. The committee did not vote on policy changes during the Oct. 14 meeting.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Moms for Liberty co-founder Tina Descovich said, "Dogs have been enriching the lives of school children across America since its founding." She called objections to dogs in the classroom "silly." 

TEXAS EDUCATION BOARD APPROVES CONTROVERSIAL CURRICULUM CHANGES TYING 'RADICAL ISLAM' TO 9/11 ATTACKS

Fox News Digital reached out to Ahmed and Ryan Scallon, superintendent of Portland Public Schools, for comment but did not immediately receive responses.

item.title: Heidi Klum leads celebs with over-the-top couples' Halloween costumes through the years
item.description: Over the years, Heidi Klum's green Medusa prosthetics stole the show, but Selena Gomez, Paris Hilton and Kourtney Kardashian also delivered iconic couples looks.
item.content:encoded:
Couples' costumes on Halloween are always fan favorites, and even more so when it's a celebrity couple.

Heidi Klum and her husband look unrecognizable on the red carpet every year in head-to-toe prosthetics, while Sarah Michelle Gellar and Freddie Prinze Jr. have referenced iconic movies from the '80s in the past.

Here are some of the best couples' Halloween costumes from over the years.

The official Queen of Halloween always goes above and beyond for her annual Halloween party, and her husband, Tom Kaulitz, plays along each year.

At her party in 2025, the couple looked unrecognizable as they posed for photos on the red carpet. Klum dressed as the Greek mythological character, Medusa, while Kaulitz dressed as a warrior she had turned into stone.

The costume consisted of a full green prosthetic bodysuit with scales and a tail following behind her, with fake teeth and a crown of snakes on top of her head, which actually moved.

"I love for people to see this and think whatever they want to think for the first time when I go on the red carpet," she told Fox News Digital in 2024. "I never like to share it before, because then people are gonna be like, ‘Oh, it wasn’t as good as I thought it was gonna be.'"

In 2024, Klum and Kaulitz arrived to the annual Halloween party dressed as different versions of E.T. from the hit '80s movie, "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial."

Kaulitz dressed as the more traditional version of E.T., while Klum dressed as the version of the character from when the kids in the movie try to disguise him, donning a black hat, blonde wig and red shawl.

"As a 9-year-old in Germany, E.T. introduced me to the idea that there’s life outside planet earth," she said on Instagram. "I know E.T. wanted to go home, but I hope that if the movie took place in 2024, that my favorite extra terrestrial would come to my party instead."

Selena Gomez and Benny Blanco were late for a very important date as they followed the white rabbit down the rabbit hole and into Wonderland for Halloween in 2024.

The couple dressed as Alice in Wonderland and the Mad Hatter, with Gomez wearing a whimsical blue dress with white socks and a blonde wig. Blanco wore black pants with a brown jacket and multicolored undershirt, paired with a big top hat and an orange wig, as he got into character with white face makeup.

"Curiouser and curiouser.." Gomez captioned the Instagram post.

Paris Hilton channeled her inner Britney Spears when she dressed as the singer in her music video for "Toxic."

The 45-year-old media personality posed for photos at the Casamigos Halloween Party in 2023 in a futuristic blue flight attendant uniform, which she paired with metallic silver-heeled boots and sunglasses.

Reum was all smiles as he stood next to her donning an airline pilot uniform.

"I’m the ghost with the most, babe," Kourtney Kardashian captioned a 2023 Instagram post featuring her and Travis Barker in their ghoulish Halloween costumes.

The celebrity couple dressed up as Beetlejuice and Lydia Deetz at their wedding. Barker wore white makeup on his face with dark circles around his eyes, paired with green hair and a burgundy red suit, perfectly capturing the essence of the spirit.

Kardashian embodied his blushing bride in a red dress with a lace neckline and sleeves, and wore her hair in an intricate updo as she posed for the photo with a serious expression and holding a bouquet of roses.

Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber embraced their inner rock stars when they dressed as David Bowie and Debbie Harry at their Halloween party in 2018.

Gerber's costume consisted of black pants and a black shirt, which he paired with a Union Jack flag coat, a red and white scarf tied around his neck and a spiky orange mullet wig. He also painted a red lightning bolt over one of his eyes to emulate Bowie's alter ego, Ziggy Stardust.

Crawford, on the other hand, wore a yellow T-shirt dress over ripped-up black tights and knee-high heeled boots with a black belt around her waist and a red handbag. She styled her hair in a big blonde wig and wore heavy eye makeup.

One of reality TV's most iconic characters dressed up as one of TV's most legendary icons, when Lisa Rinna and her husband Harry Hamlin cosplayed Lucy and Ricky Ricardo from "I Love Lucy."

Rinna channeled the comedy legend with a red wig, over-the-top makeup, a blue dress with white polka dots and a white apron. She posed for photos by pursing her lips and putting her finger up to her mouth, mimicking Lucy's classic expression.

Hamlin stood next to her wearing a suit, and raised one eyebrow as he gave the camera a serious look.

After decades together, Freddie Prinze Jr. and Sarah Michelle Gellar have had some pretty iconic couples costumes.

In 2019, the couple dressed up as Doc Brown and Marty McFly from the hit 80s movie, "Back to the Future." They shared the costume on Instagram, captioning the post, "Great Scott!!!"

The "She's All That" star wore a white jumpsuit, yellow hazmat gloves, a messy white wig with lab goggles as he posed next to Gellar, who wore jeans, a button-up shirt with denim sleeves and a red puffer vest. She accessorized with a skateboard to perfect the Marty McFly look.

The couple also recreated an iconic scene from the 1987 movie, "Dirty Dancing," choosing to dress up as characters Frances "Baby" Houseman and Johnny Castle.

In the photo, Gellar is wearing a cropped white button-up and capri denim shorts, as well as a curly short wig, as she crawled on her hands and knees towards Prinze, who was dressed as dance teacher Johnny Castle in black pants and a black tank top.

"Nobody puts baby in the corner #happyhalloween from Baby Houseman and Johnny Castle #dirtydancing #loverboy," she captioned the post.

Former couple Kelsea Ballerini and Chase Stokes were hopelessly devoted to one another when they posed for photos together at Heidi Klum's Halloween party dressed as Danny Zuko and Sandy Olsson from the movie "Grease."

The country singer's take on the iconic character included tight leather pants, an off-the-shoulder black shirt and a leather jacket, which she paired with red high heels. She styled her hair in curls and a deep side part, and got into character with red lipstick.

Stokes played the part of a greaser effortlessly in an all-black outfit, including a leather jacket with "T-Birds" written across the back. He styled his hair with a curl in the front, and accessorized with a cigarette in his mouth.

Molly Sims was ready to grant partygoers three wishes when she arrived to the Casamigos Halloween Party in 2019 dressed as Jeannie from "I Dream of Jeannie."

She channeled the iconic character in flowing sheer pink parachute pants and a pink cropped shirt with red velvet sleeves, a blonde wig tied in a high bun and a headpiece.

Her husband, Scott Stuber, also got in on the action, dressing up as Jeannie's love interest, astronaut, Tony Nelson.

item.title: How candy corn became a Halloween tradition, and why Americans still love to hate it
item.description: Candy corn was invented in the 1880s as faux chicken feed long before it became a Halloween trick-or-treating staple and polarizing holiday candy. Here's more of the history.
item.content:encoded:
Chances are high that candy corn is ending up in quite a few trick-or-treating baskets this Halloween, but the controversial confection has not always been associated with the spooky holiday.

The colorful treat has been around for more than 100 years.

It was invented in the 1880s in Philadelphia by George Renninger, an employee at Wunderle Candy Company, according to the National Confectioners Association in Washington, D.C.

HALLOWEEN CANDY FAVORITES COULD LEAVE ADULTS WITH CRACKED TEETH AND FAR WORSE, SAYS DENTIST

In keeping with a trend popular among confectioneries to make treats inspired by nature, candy corn was made to look like corn kernels.

It was initially marketed as faux chicken feed, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Candy corn’s unique layered tricolor design combined with a lack of automated machinery made for a difficult production process.

The treat became a seasonal item, with production beginning in late August and running through the fall, according to the National Confectioners Association.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Around the turn of the 20th century, another candy company, Goelitz Confectionery (now Jelly Belly Candy Company) started selling candy corn.

Although the company didn’t invent the treat, it’s widely credited for producing the candy on a larger scale and marketing it as a Halloween product.

About 35 million pounds of candy corn are produced annually, according to Farmers’ Almanac, but it’s a notoriously polarizing item.

"It's the only other candy I would hope for aside from Reese's pieces if I was trick-or-treating," a candy corn fan said on Reddit.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Another person mentioned liking the treat, but said he or she "can only have a handful at most before the sweetness is overwhelming."

Another person on Reddit was fully against candy corn, saying, "It’s disgusting. Tastes like nothing or chalk and never sweet. Don’t like the texture. Don’t like the color."

Expanding beyond the grocery store aisle, earlier this fall Brach’s, a large producer of candy corn, released a non-edible variation of the treat.

The brand debuted a limited-edition perfume, called Ode to Candy Corn, which "smells just like the iconic treat tastes," per parent company Ferrara’s website.

item.title: Pizza delivery worker's heartbreaking reaction to cruel prank sparks $680K in donations
item.description: Red Baron publicly backed its worker Walt Z. after a viral Apple Pay prank video at a Meijer store, calling him a valued team member as support poured in online.
item.content:encoded:
A video of a Red Baron pizza worker who was confronted by a prankster while on the job has gone viral, sparking a huge outpouring of support for the man from strangers and his employer alike — with the company telling Fox News Digital it stands behind its employee. 

A video that circulated online shows the worker, identified in a GoFundMe fundraiser as Walt Z., stocking frozen Red Baron pizzas in a Meijer grocery store in White Lake, Michigan, according to reports. 

The prankster is shown coming up to Walt and asking him for the time.

Then, as Walt takes out his phone to check, the person plays a sound resembling an Apple Pay transaction and claims to have stolen $10 from him, thanking him and telling him he needs to buy something.

MAN SAYS TEXAS ROADHOUSE SERVED HIM $20 STEAK INSTEAD OF PRICIER FILET MULTIPLE TIMES

Walt initially says he plans to report the prankster and becomes increasingly upset as the person insists it was just a joke.

"My life is hard enough as it is," Walt tells the prankster. 

He explains that he was already an hour late getting home, his children had already gone to bed without him and he would have to get up at 5 a.m. the next day for work. 

He also mentions that he is struggling to pay his mortgage.

APPLEBEE'S CUSTOMER PUSHES BACK ON SUGGESTED TIP AFTER CHECKING THE MATH

"I don't need this in my life," he exclaims as others try to step in.

The footage went viral on social media this week as people bashed the prankster and rallied behind the struggling father of four for pushing back on the cruel joke. 

"There’s a guy like him in every grocery store in America, grinding through the shift nobody sees," one X user wrote. 

"Turning one of them into the punchline isn’t edgy. It’s lazy."

"God bless the working man," another commenter wrote.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Fox News Digital attempted to reach Walt Z. and also reached out Red Baron. 

As of Saturday, Oct. 31, a GoFundMe campaign had raised more than $679,000 from over 19,000 donations.

The fundraiser says donations will be sent directly to Walt.

Red Baron also publicly backed its employee after the video circulated. 

The company posted on X, "He’s still here. He’s got a fan club. Including us," alongside a graphic announcing that "employee of the month nominations are closed. You know why" — suggesting that Walt might be selected for the honor.

Red Baron told Fox News Digital the incident took place in August and involved a member of its Direct Store Delivery team. 

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The company said it had checked on the employee’s well-being, continues to offer support and is working with retail partners to help maintain a safe and respectful workplace.

While internet users feared Walt could lose his job over his reaction to the incident, the company said, "We are pleased to share that he is doing well and remains a valued member of our team."

Red Baron added that Walt is grateful for the support but has requested privacy.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

In an update posted to the fundraiser, Walt thanked those who donated, shared the campaign or sent messages of support. 

He said he and his family are doing well and also asked that their privacy be respected.

"I wanted to take a moment to personally thank everyone who has donated, shared this fundraiser, or left a kind message," Walt Z. wrote on the fundraiser page.

"The kindness and encouragement you've shown me and my family have meant more than I can put into words."

item.title: Tatum O'Neal steps out with family ahead of 63rd birthday years after near-fatal stroke
item.description: Tatum O'Neal's outing with family follows years of recovery from a stroke, seizures and cardiac arrest after an overdose during the COVID-19 pandemic.
item.content:encoded:
Tatum O'Neal was recently spotted enjoying a day out with her family in Los Angeles.

The "Little Darlings" star was photographed at a fan convention with her family, wearing a black dress paired with a coat, glasses and layered necklaces. She styled her hair in an updo and walked outside the convention with the assistance of a cane.

O'Neal was accompanied by her daughter Emily McEnroe and son-in-law Tim Massarelli. 

The sighting comes ahead of the actress' 63rd birthday on Nov. 5 and more than six years after she had a near-fatal stroke in May 2020 following an overdose on morphine, opiates and pain medication.

'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR SAYS CHILD ACTORS GET 'DROPPED' AFTER HOLLYWOOD FAME FADES

In a July 2023 interview with People, O'Neal and her son, Kevin McEnroe, opened up about the health scare, with her son telling the outlet there were moments when he and his siblings, Sean and Emily "didn't think she was going to survive."

McEnroe shared that in addition to the stroke, O'Neal had multiple seizures and went into cardiac arrest. She spent six weeks in a coma.

O'Neal has struggled with drug addiction for decades, with McEnroe saying she "had become very isolated" during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, and had begun abusing medications, including some prescribed to her to treat neck and back pain and rheumatoid arthritis.

"She had become very isolated," he told People. "With the addition of morphine and heavier pharmaceuticals, it was getting scary. COVID, chronic pain, all these things led to a place of isolation. In that place, I don't think, for her, there was much hope."

O'Neal made her feature film debut in the 1973 movie, "Paper Moon," which she starred in alongside her famous father, Ryan O'Neal, at nine years old.

She went on to make history for her role in the film, as the youngest winner of a competitive Academy Award, when she took home the award for best supporting actress at the 46th Academy Awards in 1974, when she was 10 years old.

"All I really want to thank is my director Peter Bogdanovich and my father. Thank you," she said in her acceptance speech.

While she thanked her father in her speech, the two went on to have a turbulent relationship. In her 2004 autobiography, "A Paper Life," Tatum shared that their relationship first became rocky after making "Paper Moon," because he was jealous of her success.

In the book, she also alleged he physically and emotionally abused her, and said he was addicted to drugs.

Ryan O'Neal died in December 2023 at the age of 82 from congestive heart failure, and in a February 2025 interview with Variety, Tatum shared her reaction to being left out of his will, noting she only learned of the decision following his death.

"Keep it, motherf-----," she said. "The first book that I wrote was just a f---ing honest book. And that’s what got him."

item.title: Major US children's hospital opens historic detransition clinic after $10M legal showdown
item.description: Ken Paxton announced Texas Children's Hospital opened the nation's first detransition clinic as part of a settlement over gender care practices.
item.content:encoded:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced Tuesday that the nation’s first-ever detransition clinic has opened at Texas Children’s Hospital following a $10 million settlement with the state.

The announcement comes after Paxton reached a settlement with TCH in May, finalized in August, requiring the hospital to pay $10 million to resolve government claims and separately establish and fund a detransition clinic. The new clinic provides "detransition-related medical care to patients through age 21, along with detransition-related obstetric and gynecologic care to patients older than 21," according to Paxton's office.

"In accordance with my settlement with Texas Children’s Hospital, the nation’s first-ever Detransition Clinic is now open," Paxton said in a statement. "I will continue to ensure that this clinic provides the care and support that victims of the radical left’s gender ideology deserve."

A LANDMARK TEXAS RULING BREATHES NEW LIFE INTO ONE DETRANSITIONER'S QUEST FOR JUSTICE

"Together, we will protect our children and defeat the dangerous ideology that has inflicted irreversible harm on innocent kids," he continued.

Tuesday's announcement comes as Paxton is running for election in Texas' 2026 Senate race. President Donald Trump campaigned in two separate Texas cities, Corpus Christi and Lubbock, on Tuesday in an effort to boost Paxton's Senate bid.

The Trump administration has been targeting initiatives related to transgender people in recent months. Trump announced in August that his administration will cease providing funding for gender transition surgeries using Medicaid for minors.

Paxton's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

A TCH spokesperson told Fox News Digital on Wednesday that the hospital prioritizes providing patients "the highest standard of care," including through the detransition clinic.

"First and foremost, patients and families are at the center of all we do and we will always provide the highest standard of care, including through this clinic, which formalizes the supportive, multidisciplinary services we have and will continue to deliver," the TCH spokesperson said. "Given the multidisciplinary approach, care may be delivered in multiple locations, depending on individual patient needs."

"All services provided will be within our hospital’s existing licensure and scope," the spokesperson added. "Services will include Endocrinology, Surgery, Primary Care, Fertility Counseling, Psychiatry, Psychology, Social Work/Case Management and Speech Pathology. The clinic is operational and we are complying with all requirements in the settlement agreement."

The TCH spokesperson also told Fox News Digital that the hospital is "actively triaging prospective patients" for the detransition clinic.

"Protecting the privacy of our patients and their families is a top priority, thus we are unable to share patient information," the spokesperson stated. "We are actively triaging prospective patients through our established intake process. We can tell you that thus far, we have not yet had clinical appointments with patients."

INSURANCE COMPANIES PUT ON NOTICE FOR STRANDING TRANS PATIENTS WHO WANT TO REVERSE SURGERIES

TCH is required to fully fund services provided through the detransition clinic for its first five years, ensuring patients receive those services at no cost, and must also publicize the clinic on its website, per the settlement.

The May settlement also required TCH to pay $10 million to resolve claims brought under the Texas Health Care Program Fraud Prevention Act and the federal False Claims Act over allegations that the hospital improperly billed Texas Medicaid for gender-transition treatments, according to Paxton's office.

Do No Harm, a medical advocacy organization critical of gender-transition treatments for minors, estimates that 13,994 minors received gender-transition-related medical interventions between 2019 and 2023, based on its analysis of insurance claims data.

A Fox News poll published on Oct. 21 found that Democratic candidate James Talarico and Paxton were tied at 49% each among likely voters in the Lone Star State.

item.title: 'Baywatch' star Nicole Eggert exposes financial toll of cancer battle: 'The bills don't stop'
item.description: Nicole Eggert reveals the financial toll of her breast cancer battle as a single parent, from lost income to mounting bills during treatment.
item.content:encoded:
Nicole Eggert admitted that finances are a neglected conversation when it comes to fighting cancer.

Eggert, 54, was diagnosed with stage 2 cribriform carcinoma breast cancer in December 2023. Two years later, the actress revealed her cancer status was "NED," or no evidence of disease.

While the "Baywatch" star is a survivor of a club she "never wanted to be a part of," Eggert told Fox News Digital that the financial strains of her battle added an entirely different stressor to her life.

BRANDI GLANVILLE SPEAKS OUT ON COMPLEX DIAGNOSIS AND $6K MONTHLY MEDICAL BATTLE

"I'm a 100% single parent," Eggert explained. "One of my daughters is an adult, so she is very self-independent, and she does great, but I do have a teenager still at home ... I have that responsibility, and then I have all the household and homemaker, head of household responsibilities and then the cost of what this diagnosis brings, which is a lot ... really you can't even wrap your head around it."

‘BAYWATCH’ STAR NICOLE EGGERT SAYS IT'S ‘VERY HARD TO BE HEALTHY IN AMERICA’ AS SHE BATTLES CANCER

Eggert noted that the costs consistently "add up," so much so that she was afraid of being able to provide for her family.

"In my line of work, I couldn't commit to being on any kind of production because I'm gonna be in treatment and in and out of treatment ... three-to-five at least days a week," she said. "So, it's not like it's work from home kind of work."

She added, "I had to completely come to the realization that I wasn't gonna have income, and yet the bills don't stop, and the teenagers still need their things, and life needs their things and the car still needs the gas, and you know, all of it."

The "Charles in Charge" actress noted that when she took a step back and truly looked at the disease, "money seemed very trivial."

LINDA PERRY SAYS SHE WAS FEELING HEALTHY WHEN DOCTORS DISCOVERED ‘ANGRY’ CANCER BY CHANCE

"It's sort of like, well, 'Ah, I'm alive.' Then, you know, if you have any kind of financial strain, it's like, 'Well, at least you're alive to deal with it,'" she said. "At least you are alive where you can go out and fix it."

She added, "So there's that part too, where suddenly you're like, 'Wow, whatever. It's just it's just money.' And that comes and goes. So, you know, it's ebb and flow of life."

In December 2023, after experiencing unexplained weight gain and pain in her left breast, Eggert was diagnosed with a rare form of breast cancer.

She underwent her first mastectomy soon after, and later explained that she'd wanted to do a double mastectomy at the time, but her doctor advised that if she just had one breast removed, she'd be able to get into treatment faster, and her immune system wouldn't take as big a hit, so she agreed.

WATCH: 'Baywatch' star Nicole Eggert details financial toll of cancer battle

Over a year later, in August 2025, she had her other breast removed, and surgeons performed a reconstruction.

Eggert admitted that one major component in her cancer journey was being able to rely on community.

"You really have to find your community, and you really have to be OK with asking for help or asking other people how they do it, and getting tips and tricks and just all the information you can get," she said. "That's why these conversations are just so, so important and so necessary. Because what else would you do?"

As part of Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Eggert partnered with Novartis and shared a little more insight into her cancer journey on the Voices of MORE podcast with Amy Robach and Dr. Helen Coons.

Eggert explained how helpful it can be for women to get together, share stories and find interwoven commonality in experiences.

"If we keep talking about these things, it becomes so much easier to talk about, and maybe we don't feel like we have to hide things anymore because in the past it's not ... it's kind of been a taboo topic," she said. "And now I think more and more women are becoming more comfortable to discuss what their journey looks like, what it feels like, how it's gone for them."

While the past has its place, Eggert is looking forward to the future and spending more time enjoying life to the fullest with her family.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I also am really looking forward to stepping back into life not having to be in treatment or in the treatment facility with this newfound power and fearlessness that I have, and this new appreciation for life that I have, and It's like this second chance at life," she said.

"I know that that's so cliche, but it's to jump back in with all of these crazy changes that have happened in the past two years, three years. There's been very, very big changes inside myself."

She added, "So to be able to now go back into life and get back into the workforce and get back into doing things I enjoy with this new mindset, it's exciting. It's exciting!"

item.title: Riley Gaines, Kat Timpf push back after 'Call Her Daddy' host suggests wives can always find better partners
item.description: Riley Gaines and Kat Timpf fire back at Alex Cooper's "Call Her Daddy" marriage advice, arguing the grass is always greener where you water it.
item.content:encoded:
Riley Gaines and Kat Timpf pushed back against podcaster Alex Cooper's advice on leaving a marriage this week, responding to the "Call Her Daddy" host's assertion that women can always find better partners.

Speaking on Fox News' "The Girls" podcast, Gaines and Timpf argued that women should focus on investing in their marriages rather than assuming they can find better partners elsewhere.

"To kind of combat the narrative that's out there that we just heard from Alex Cooper, 'seek more, seek better, it's the patriarchy,' which is of course just intentionally using buzzwords," Gaines said.

JESSIE JAMES DECKER ON WHY HER MARRIAGE TO ERIC DECKER HASN'T LOST ITS SPARK AFTER FOUR KIDS

"The grass is not always greener on the other side. I have found, at least in my marriage, it's greener where you water it. Pouring into your husband, allowing him to pour into you, that's where I've seen growth," she added.

The "Call Her Daddy" episode was released earlier this month and featured Cooper and actress Sophia Bush, whose 2023 divorce from entrepreneur Grant Hughes made headlines. The two discussed women who hesitate to leave a marriage out of fear that they cannot find a better partner, a concern both Cooper and Bush dismissed.

GROWING TREND OF HATING MEN BACKFIRES AS ANTI-MARRIAGE CULTURE LEAVES SINGLE WOMEN LOSING OUT

"That's such a beautiful message to leave women with because I do think we can get really, really in our heads about, 'Oh my God, I feel like I'm, maybe I shouldn't leave this marriage because can I even get better?'" Cooper said. "And the answer is always yes."

Bush agreed, saying, "And this idea that it's too late or you're too old or who are you to want more? That's patriarchy. That is crazy. We don't need it."

POLITICAL FIGHTS CAN RIP COUPLES APART — THERAPIST SHARES 3 WAYS TO SAVE A RELATIONSHIP

Timpf challenged Cooper's advice, pointing to her husband's support during some of the most difficult experiences of her life.

"I also couldn't disagree more with what she said because, first of all, she said you can always do better than your husband. That's not true," Timpf said.

MATTHEW MCCONAUGHEY'S PIECE OF RELATIONSHIP ADVICE THAT KEEPS HIS MARRIAGE TO CAMILA ALVES STRONG

"I know that I can't do better than my husband because I mean, he's hot and all that. But also just, I mean I can't do better than the guy that held my hand through cancer, through childbirth, then my father's funeral," she added.

Timpf said some people find it controversial when she says her marriage is the most important thing in her life.

TRADITIONAL TWO-PARENT FAMILIES VANISH FROM BIG AMERICAN CITIES AS 'MARRIAGE DESERTS' EXPAND

"There's nothing more important in my life than my marriage," Timpf said. "And people say, 'But what about your kids?' It's like, 'Okay, but it's for my kids that I have that opinion.' Because if you do not make time as a couple and see each other as a couple and keep that going, then that's not good for the family either."

item.title: Bill Maher hits back at Trump over blistering Truth Social post, jokes about president's dinner review
item.description: Bill Maher fired back at Trump's record 1,300-word Truth Social post on "Real Time," reading the president's attacks aloud line by line onstage.
item.content:encoded:
Comedian Bill Maher mocked a lengthy Truth Social post from President Donald Trump, in which the president reversed course on his assessment of the pair's second dinner at the White House.

During Friday's episode of HBO's "Real Time," Maher mocked Trump's 1,300-word Truth Social post, which criticized the comedian after their second White House dinner earlier this month.

"Did you see the 1,300-word tweet he sent out? Longest ever! Kind of a flex," Maher said. "I tell you, dining at the White House is the opposite of the Cheesecake Factory: After you leave, they review you. He went off on me like Kelly Clarkson in a toy store."

BILL MAHER FIRES BACK AT LIBERAL CRITICS OVER SECOND TRUMP DINNER

Maher went on to hold up a copy of Trump’s post — his longest ever to Truth Social — while insisting that the "whole point" of dining with Trump is so the two men can discuss their differences in a civil setting.

"And then, I go back to my job here, and then, the heartaches begin," he added.

BILL MAHER CLAIMS DONALD TRUMP FELT 'BETRAYED' BY HIM WITH 'SILLY' FEUD AFTER CORDIAL 2025 DINNER

Maher then read portions of the post to the audience to "address a few of the allegations" before jokingly agreeing with Trump’s assessment that he is a "complete and total loser."

"He talks about how I call him incessantly. I’ve never called you. You call me," Maher said. "I’d be afraid to call you. You’re the president, I’d think you’re too busy. Well, plainly not."

BILL MAHER REVEALS HE'S HAVING DINNER WITH TRUMP AGAIN, SAYS HE WAS 'REALLY NICE' BY TEXT

Maher also disputed Trump's claim that he "invited himself to the White House," joking, "As if you could do that. 'Sir, Bill Maher is here. Well, he's not invited, but it's the law.'"

MAHER MOCKS LIBERALS FOR STILL PANICKING ABOUT TRUMP'S ANTICS, PERSONALITY AFTER 10 YEARS

Maher complained that Trump "doesn't even notice what I actually say." After reading Trump's assertion that he "doesn't even think it was a good thing to take the nuclear weapon away from Iran," the HBO host played clips of himself supporting U.S. military strikes against Iran. Maher then joked, "So am I smart now?"

Maher laughed as he read Trump's final assessment of the dinner: "I love this, 'Overall, I thought it was a good meeting.'"

Maher laughed as he read Trump's final assessment of the dinner: "I love this, 'Overall, I thought it was a good meeting.'"

The exchange followed Maher and Trump's second White House dinner on Oct. 15, which musician Kid Rock and ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith also attended.

KID ROCK DETAILS SIT-DOWN WITH TRUMP, STEPHEN A SMITH AND BILL MAHER

"The dinner last night with Kid Rock and Stephen A. [Smith] and Bill Maher was great," Trump told reporters after the dinner. "I think they had a good time."

The president added that Maher "likes me a lot more than people understand."

STEPHEN A SMITH DEFENDS WHITE HOUSE DINNER WITH TRUMP

Trump and Maher have had a contentious relationship, but Axia Public Relations CEO Jason Mudd told Fox News Digital that Maher responded to the president's criticism with poise, even as the two offered conflicting accounts of their latest dinner.

"Humor answers an attack without escalating it. If Bill Maher were my client, I'd advise him to aim the jokes at the situation and away from the individual," Mudd said. "Reading the attack aloud, line by line, signals confidence. It tells the audience he read every word and still stayed calm. In most public disputes, the calmest voice wins the news cycle."

Fox News Digital reached out to Maher and the White House for comment.

item.title: Who are Ilhan Omar’s lawyers? Meet the high-powered Dem attorneys the embattled rep hired
item.description: Ilhan Omar has hired Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, attorneys who represented Biden, House Democrats in Trump impeachment, and E. Jean Carroll.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has tapped two high-powered Washington, D.C.-based attorneys who have previously represented elected officials at the highest echelon of American politics.

Amid dueling federal investigations — one for immigration fraud and another for financial disclosure discrepancies — the embattled Somali-born lawmaker hired Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, according to a CBS report, both of whom are partners at Hecker Fink LLP.

The attorneys have in the past represented Democrat clients and taken on left-leaning cases — especially those taking aim at President Donald Trump, his administration and his supporters.

ILHAN OMAR'S TURBULENT WEEK EXPLAINED: THE DUELING PROBES THAT THREW THE SOMALI-BORN PROGRESSIVE INTO CHAOS

Jeffress is a former federal prosecutor whose biography says she tried more than 40 cases during a decade in the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the District of Columbia, where she was Chief of the National Security Section. She has also been a Department of Justice (DOJ) Attaché.

She served as former President Joe Biden's attorney in his lawsuit against the DOJ earlier this year. In that case, Biden sought to halt the release of audio recordings between himself and his "Promise Me, Dad" book ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer. The audio was recorded in 2016 and 2017, and were subject to a FOIA request from the Heritage Foundation in 2024.

They were cited during special counsel Robert Hur's investigation into whether Biden illegally retained classified information from his term as vice president, and piqued the interest of conservatives demanding answers about Biden's mental acuity.

The court declined to block the release of the recordings where Biden ad frequent memory lapses, and they were made public in July.

FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE

Before her time at Hecker Fink, Jeffress, a Yale Law graduate from 1992, served as counsel for then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and the Democrat-led House January 6 committee, which spent two years investigating the riot at the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021. She represented the committee when it was sued by a Trump campaign spokesperson, Taylor Budowich, after the committee subpoenaed his bank records.

Jeffress also represented Trump foe and former FBI attorney Lisa Page — a key figure in the left's Russiagate conspiracy theory — during congressional scrutiny into the FBI's handling of the matter. Page later sued the DOJ for releasing her text messages with her then-FBI colleague and lover Peter Strzok.

In the messages, Strzok assuaged Page's concerns that Trump would become president by vowing that the FBI would stop it, and referred to an "insurance policy" against his presidency. That case was settled in 2024.

ILHAN OMAR'S WEALTH SCANDAL TAKES A TURN JUST ONE DAY AFTER RAID OF HER DC HOME

Jeffress is married to U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper of the District of Washington, D.C., who in May ruled that it was illegal for the the John F. Kennedy Performing Arts Center to add Trump's name. Trump publicly criticized Cooper as "highly conflicted," due to his relationship with Jeffress.

Matz is also a partner at Hecker Fink. He graduated from Harvard Law, and clerked for former Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy.

"Joshua’s practice has long included a focus on democracy and elections," his biography page says.

He represented the state of Pennsylvania in defending the certification of its election results, including arguing before the Supreme Court.

ILHAN OMAR’S EMBATTLED HUSBAND APPEARS AT SCENE OF HSI RAID IN MIDST OF CRIMINAL FRAUD INVESTIGATION

He was counsel to House Democrats during both failed impeachment attempts against Trump during his first term in office.

Matz also represented E. Jean Carroll in two separate civil cases against Trump related to his denial of her of sexual assault claims against him. He was never criminally charged. In 2022, Carroll accused Trump of defaming her in his denial of her account of an incident she claims happened in 1996. A New York jury found Trump liable for defamation and for sexual assault.

Prior to that case, in 2019, a jury awarded Carroll $83.3 million for defamation stemming from other comments made by Trump.

Matz represented students, parents and teachers who opposed Florida's Parental Rights in Education Act, which his biography describes as the "Don't Say Gay" law, which restricted teaching students about sexual orientation and gender identity.

He also successfully represented Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear when he was sued for COVID-19 lockdowns, including school closures, and victims of the 2017 "Unite the Right" rally in Charlottesville.

Now, Matz and Jeffress are representing Omar as she seeks to battle two federal probes. In a video message posted to her social media earlier this month, the lawmaker pleaded with her supporters to keep sending money, noting that her fight against the investigations would be costly.

Omar's attorneys did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Neither did the White House.

item.title: Human vs ChatGPT NFL Week 8 betting picks: Human answers with 4-1 week, looks to keep rolling

item.content:encoded:

BUFFALO BILLS TAP HOMETOWN HEROES GOO GOO DOLLS FOR THANKSGIVING NIGHT HALFTIME CONCERT

I prefer the over, which made my card, but the hook makes Baltimore appealing: a three-point Buffalo victory still cashes this ticket.

The Jags are coming off a bye after back-to-back London weeks, so I see their offense starting slowly in this one. The Colts can’t really score at all, just traded Quenton Nelson and are looking to trade Josh Downs and Jonathan Taylor. With all the uncertainty around a team that already has offensive problems, it’s hard to see where the points are going to come from. Jacksonville’s defense was playing really well before the second London game, when it gave up 34 points against Houston, but the Colts are a perfect bounce-back spot.

Los Angeles Chargers at Los Angeles Rams, Sunday at 4:05 p.m. ET

item.title: New York and LA didn't win America's best mega airport title, but one Midwest hub did
item.description: Coastal airports were outpaced as J.D. Power named Minneapolis the top mega hub for a third year, while Tampa and Charleston led their categories amid rising satisfaction scores.
item.content:encoded:
A Midwestern airport has once again come out on top among North America’s largest hubs, outpacing better-known coastal airports serving New York and Los Angeles.

Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport topped the mega airport category for the third consecutive year, according to new 2026 rankings from J.D. Power of North America’s best airports.

Tampa International Airport and Charleston International Airport also took top honors in their respective size categories, the same survey found. 

DEADLY DISEASE SPARKS NEW CDC RULE FOR US-BOUND FLYERS AS MAJOR AIRLINES SEEK DELAY

"Minneapolis does a lot of things well," Gary Leff, a Texas-based travel industry expert and author of the blog "View From the Wing," told Fox News Digital.

"Connecting passengers have plenty of amenities without having to leave security," Leff said. "Local passengers have an airport relatively close to both downtowns, with light rail access."

Leff said Minneapolis passengers may face long walks between gates, but he said it still feels manageable.

The airport's score was 684 on J.D. Power's 1,000-point scale. 

Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport ranked second among mega airports with 663 points, followed by Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport with 642.

POPULAR AIRLINE HITS CUSTOMERS WITH STEEP FEE HIKE FOR FIRST TIME IN 8 YEARS

Tampa ranked first among large airports with a score of 715, followed by Portland International Airport with 708 and Dallas Love Field with 698.

Charleston led the medium-airport category with 712 points, ahead of Ontario International Airport with 705 and Indianapolis International Airport with 695.

"Tampa is very well organized, even though you do have to transit between your concourses," Leff said.

Charleston is not overbuilt, he said, so it's easy to get through the airport.

TRAVEL NIGHTMARE UNFOLDS AS MAJOR AIRLINE SCRAPS FLIGHT AFTER HARROWING 12-HOUR DELAY

"What is an airport for? An airport is a place that you go to get to, through and out of quickly. You're flying, you're trying to go somewhere very efficiently. The best airports are the ones that help you do exactly that," Leff said.

Overall passenger satisfaction increased across all three airport categories.

J.D. Power, headquartered in Troy, Michigan, said all the highest-ranked airports have recently completed, or are close to completing, multiyear capital improvement projects.

"On the whole, those efforts are finally starting to pay off in the form of higher overall passenger satisfaction scores," Michael Taylor, managing director of travel, hospitality and retail at J.D. Power, said in a statement.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Leff cautioned travelers, however, not to get too swayed by upscale renovations. 

"New York LaGuardia's Central Terminal is a beautiful facility … but it is still … an airport that is relatively difficult to get through," Leff noted.

New York and Los Angeles missed the mark, and Leff was not surprised.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Leff believes San Francisco International Airport and National Airport in Washington, D.C. are among the country’s best because they are close to their cities and easy to navigate.

The study identified clear signage and easy navigation as major drivers of satisfaction.

Food, beverage and retail programs improved, rising 8 points year over year.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The North America Airport Satisfaction Study is in its 21st year and measures passenger experiences across seven areas: ease of travel through the airport, trust in the airport, terminal facilities, airport staff, the departure or trip-to-airport experience, food, beverage and retail, and the arrival or trip-from-airport experience, according to the company. 

J.D. Power said it defines mega airports as those with at least 33 million passengers per year, large airports as those with 10 million to 32.9 million passengers and medium airports as those with 4.5 million to 9.9 million passengers.

The 2026 study is based on 24,710 completed surveys from U.S. and Canadian residents who traveled through at least one U.S. or Canadian airport.

item.title: Political activism, antisemitism allegations put public schools under the microscope
item.description: Philadelphia and Los Angeles public schools face allegations of pushing one-sided Israeli-Palestinian conflict views and antisemitic content in classrooms.
item.content:encoded:
Public schools in both Philadelphia and Los Angeles are facing scrutiny over allegations that educators used classroom and student activities to push politics on controversial topics, including the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The cases have raised fresh concerns among advocates about the infiltration of political activism in education.

The House Education and Workforce Committee found in Philadelphia that district curricula endorsed "ideology justifying violent resistance and legitimize radical groups that incite antisemitism." Meanwhile, in Los Angeles, the school district substantiated 11 allegations involving teachers at Canoga Park High School, finding that they promoted one-sided views about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Jewish Insider reported. The complaints were brought by the North American Values Institute, or NAVI.

"NAVI is very active in tracking what extremists are doing in education. And so, when we started seeing Code Pink do webinars discussing sort of what they were up to in Los Angeles County schools, we paid very close attention," NAVI Government Affairs Director Clifford Smith told Fox News Digital. 

FEDS OPEN PROBE INTO ANTI-ISRAEL NYC TEACHERS

"When we saw that they were making plans to basically directly insert, you know, very politicized... far, far, far-left propaganda directly in the classrooms, we wanted to act because we knew that, you know, at least according to the rules of the school district, that shouldn't happen," Smith said. 

The Los Angeles Unified School District's (LAUSD) investigation found that high school teachers had been giving one-sided lessons on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including a lesson on the "martyrs of Gaza," according to Jewish Insider. The outlet noted that the investigation also revealed that teachers had been recruiting students to join the anti-Israel group Students for Justice in Palestine.

Following the investigation, LAUSD adopted several corrective measures, including removing political materials from classes, restructuring curricula and requiring staff training on antisemitism and political advocacy rules, according to Jewish Insider.

NATION’S LARGEST TEACHERS UNION UNDER FIRE AS CONTROVERSIAL AGENDA PUTS CENTURY-OLD FEDERAL CHARTER AT RISK

Corey DeAngelis, a research fellow at the Heritage Foundation, said the corrective measures did not address what he described as the broader culture behind the allegations.

"Legal remedies and corrective actions do not fix the root of the problem," DeAngelis told Fox News Digital. "Removing materials, restructuring some curricula, and requiring training marks a step in the right direction. Yet the underlying bias, ideology, and hostile environment remain embedded in the public school system as long as the same staff, the same culture, and the same monopoly persist."

Tina Descovich, CEO and co-founder of Moms for Liberty, said the findings in Los Angeles were "deeply troubling."

"Teachers actively pushed antisemitic viewpoints and anti-Israel prejudice on young, impressionable children," Descovich told Fox News Digital. "This should never happen in America. And yet not only is it occurring daily, but teachers unions are actively running cover for it."

ACTIVIST TEACHER’S PALESTINIAN IDENTITY CLAIMS UNRAVEL AS SHE ADMITS BEING A ‘WHITE WOMAN’ OF PRIVILEGE

Smith said the issue was not whether teachers discussed the conflict, but rather how they presented it.

"Now, I have no problem teaching both sides of any conflict. I do have a problem with anybody teaching entirely one side of a conflict without teaching the others or entirely one side of the debate without teaching the other sides of the debate," Smith told Fox News Digital.

In Philadelphia, according to the congressional committee, students were asked as part of a world history unit to create artwork that "embodies the concept of cultural resistance." The committee's report also stated that students were taught the definition of "settler colonialism," which was described as having "taken place across many areas throughout the world."

The committee also found that students were instructed to "honor" a resistance movement of their choosing. The list of movements provided to the students included the Great March of Return, a Hamas campaign that included deadly clashes.

In a statement provided to Fox News Digital, the School District of Philadelphia said, "Antisemitism has no place in our schools, and we take concerns about antisemitic harassment or discrimination very seriously, just as we do not condone or tolerate Islamophobia, racism, or discrimination against any ethnic, racial or religious group."

Additionally, the School District of Philadelphia provided a statement from the Board of Education to Fox News Digital, stating that it disagrees with the committee's report and remains "committed to fostering school climates where all students and staff feel supported and safe."

UNEARTHED FILING SHOWS LARGEST TEACHERS UNIONS POURED OVER $900 MILLION INTO POLITICAL ACTIVITIES

During a September interview with the House Education and Workforce Committee, Superintendent of the School District of Philadelphia Dr. Tony B. Watlington said that controversial topics had to be addressed in ways that are "age appropriate and consistent with our belief that we teach students how to think and not what to think."

For some Jewish families, the handling of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict expanded beyond the classroom and into the general school environment.

Nataliya, a mother whose children go to school in the Philadelphia metro area, told Fox News Digital that it was important to her that her children grew up in a place where they could feel safe being openly Jewish.

"Being safe as a Jew and being safe to be a Jew was very important to me because of my background," Nataliya, who is a Jewish immigrant from the Soviet Union, told Fox News Digital. She added that she and her husband agreed to live in an area with strong public schools where their children could be comfortable being Jewish. However, things changed after Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attacks in Israel, according to Nataliya.

Nataliya said that two of her middle-school-aged son's teachers, who happened to be Jewish, claimed that they, independent of each other, opted for old Q&A sessions in their classrooms after Oct. 7 and both were reprimanded. She said the teacher informed her that they had been "told they were not allowed to say anything about October 7 or to answer any questions if they ask them anything."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

After that, Nataliya and her husband decided to move their son to a Jewish private school. They decided that their daughter would finish elementary school before moving to a private school.

Nataliya's decision to move her son out of public school is one that Sydney Altfield, CEO of Teach Coalition, said she is hearing from other Jewish families as well.

"When antisemitism is going on in public schools, students feel unsafe and we know this happens. Students feel unsafe there, and they flee to Jewish day schools," Altfield told Fox News Digital.

She explained that, while Jewish private schools, often referred to as "day schools," are expensive, communities and schools will often come together to help families with the financial burden. However, there is another cost that Jewish schools have faced: security.

"We found that schools after October 7 are spending over $400,000 a year on security funding. So all of these things add up... and it really is a domino effect," Altfield said. "When kids are feeling unsafe in a public school, and they choose to move to a Jewish day school, costs for that day school go up. Support for that community goes up. It's really a long-term effect, and we track all of this – enrollment tuition, security expenses, everything."

Altfield, whose organization focuses on private schools, told Fox News Digital that she did not think that antisemitism would reach these levels in her lifetime.

"We are living in an alternate universe of the world that I grew up in, in the world that, you know, we all want to grow up in," she said, adding that the issue of antisemitism is on both sides of the political aisle. 

"We must do everything to stop it, and if that means we have to build more Jewish day schools to keep ourselves safe, then we're going to make sure that our community is safe no matter what," Atfield said. 

Fox News Digital reached out to LAUSD for comment but did not immediately hear back.

item.title: Commanders lose Pro Bowl defensive tackle Daron Payne for the season after suffering practice injury: report

item.content:encoded:
The Washington Commanders had a bye last week, but the injuries didn’t stop.

Pro Bowl defensive tackle Daron Payne suffered a season-ending Jones fracture at practice Friday, according to ESPN.

For the reeling Commanders, it’s a crushing blow. Payne has been an anchor on their defensive line since being drafted with the No. 13 overall pick in the 2018 NFL Draft out of Alabama.

In six games this season, the Pro Bowl tackle has recorded 14 tackles and one sack. Across his nine-year career, Payne has 446 tackles and 38 sacks in 136 games.

Losing Payne for the rest of the season is a blow that the 1-4-1 Commanders might not be able to handle. The Commanders were already yielding 28.7 points per game with him in the lineup, the second-worst mark in the NFL. Only the Arizona Cardinals have a worse scoring defense (29.7 points per game).

One area in which the Commanders' defense was about average was against the run, as it allowed 100.5 rushing yards per game, good for 14th in the NFL. However, without Payne, that number will likely rise.

item.title: James Madison fans were warned about Billy Napier, now the chickens have come home to roost
item.description: Billy Napier's James Madison Dukes blew huge leads in back-to-back overtime losses, and Florida Gators fans say they warned JMU all along.
item.content:encoded:
A little less than two weeks ago, the James Madison Dukes were one of the toasts of the college football world.

The Sun Belt darlings were 7-0, and new head coach Billy Napier looked like he had exorcised all of the demons that plagued him at his previous stop in the Sunshine State.

The Dukes were lighting up the scoreboard, and talks of a College Football Playoff appearance were starting to crop up all around Harrisonburg.

EX-FLORIDA GATORS COACH BILLY NAPIER RIPPED TO SHREDS BY FORMER PLAYER DURING PODCAST APPEARANCE

Since then, the mood has soured considerably in the Shenandoah Valley, thanks to a two-game losing streak that has effectively ended any CFP dreams that purple and gold-clad fans had swirling around in their heads.

But it isn't just the number in the loss column that has JMU fans vexed, it's how those losses happened and who they happened against that is causing all of the consternation.

WHY ONE DETAIL ABOUT NFL FINAL ROSTERS PROVES FORMER FLORIDA COACH BILLY NAPIER WAS WORSE THAN YOU REMEMBER

Both games were almost identical to one another in terms of how they went, as the Dukes were healthy favorites against both Appalachian State and Troy and raced out to considerable first half leads before stagnating in the second half, losing both games in overtime.

What's even more damning is that the second half swoons have been happening quite a bit this year, with James Madison being outscored in the final 30+ minutes in four of the eight games they've played against FBS competition.

A COMBINATION OF BAD COACHING HIRES AND SUBPAR QUARTERBACK PLAY IS THE CULPRIT FOR SEC'S RECENT SWOON

In other words, this isn't a new development.

If only someone could have warned Dukes fans before they hired a guy like Napier.

Oh wait...

If you read my buddy and fellow Gator fan Zach Dean's latest edition of Nightcaps, you're already aware that there is somewhat of a mea culpa happening on social media between James Madison fans and Florida supporters.

LOYALTY BE DAMNED: DID THESE COACHES STICK AROUND A SEASON TOO LONG AND BLOW THEIR CHANCES AT A BIG GIG?

My Orange and Blue brethren spent all offseason repeatedly cautioning the JMU faithful about Napier's tendencies and pig-headed nature when it came to coaching.

Dukes fans were confident the issues had been fixed, even pointing to the fact that a self-reflective Napier went on a speaking tour talking about how he "looked in the mirror" and took ownership of how things fell apart in Gainesville.

He even hired an offensive coordinator, something he was practically begged to do for four years while coaching at Florida.

The national media got on board, too, wondering if Florida really was just some toxic situation where even the best coaches went to kill their careers.

The media and Dukes fans even doubled down when JMU got off to that aforementioned 7-0 start.

Then it all came crashing down, and the same issues that sank Napier in The Swamp reared their ugly head in the Commonwealth.

Poor clock management, stagnant second half offenses, head-scratching play calls in high-leverage situations.

You can find a handful of Florida games from 2022-25 that resemble the two most recent JMU losses to a T, so much so that many Gator fans were accurately predicting what would happen next.

A tiger can't change its stripes, and although Napier went out and hired an OC and did some reflecting in the offseason, this is who he is.

In his final season at Louisiana as the head coach of the Ragin' Cajuns, Napier uttered the now infamous "scared money don't make money" catchphrase that made him a hot candidate during the 2021 hiring cycle.

Ironically, every coaching moment for Billy after that has been the definition of "scared money."

This latest masterpiece sums it all up perfectly.

Napier coaches with a style that offers the lowest possible margin for error.

It's why, even in games he was dominating while at Florida, the game would always usually come down to one score in the fourth quarter.

His swan song in The Swamp, a shocking 29-21 upset over then-top-10 Texas, saw the Gators bludgeoning the Longhorns on both lines of scrimmage.

Any coach worth his salt would have put his foot on Texas' throat and put the Longhorns away early, but Napier and company "turtled" in the second half, making a few boneheaded decisions in the process, to allow the Bevo Boys to have a chance to tie the game late in the fourth.

And perhaps the worst part of it all is who came before Napier at James Madison.

The coaches directly preceding Billy in Harrisonburg were Curt Cignetti and Bob Chesney, two of the most calculated, ruthlessly efficient coaches in the game of college football right now.

Everything they did made sense from an analytics standpoint, and their teams were (and are) well coached and almost never "play with their food."
